reader.title: Attempted lynching of Sylvester Grubb
bases: Crowds from Downey's neighborhood twice set out for the Princeton jail and sixty masked, armed men later searched a train to seize Grubb, an accused murderer in custody, with the stated plan to hang him (A4, A6, A10).

Groups of three or more (sixty men at Francisco) sought to seize and hang Grubb for the shooting of Gertrude Downey, but officials kept him away from them and he was later tried and sentenced to death in court (A6, A10, A11); no one was killed by the mob.

The Indianapolis Journal's Princeton and Evansville specials, the Vincennes and Princeton wire reports of the train search, the Jasper Weekly Courier and the Journal's trial report independently agree that mobs sought Grubb and that he was moved to avoid them (A4, A6, A9, A11, A12).

summary.text: The attempted lynching of Sylvester Grubb consisted of mob efforts in Gibson County, Indiana, in September and October 1888 to seize and hang Grubb, who was accused of shooting Gertrude Downey at the Princeton fair grounds.
Officials kept Grubb out of reach by moving him to Evansville and Jeffersonville, and a mob of sixty masked men that searched a train for him at Francisco found the wrong train.
Grubb was instead tried in the Knox Circuit Court at Vincennes and sentenced to death.
According to the trial testimony as reported from Vincennes, Grubb, 24, had courted Downey for about two years, and after she refused to marry him he wrote her a letter vowing revenge.
On Thursday, Sept. 13, he followed her to the Princeton fair, led her toward an unfrequented part of the grounds and was accused of shooting her in the face and arm.
He was arrested on the spot after snapping the revolver at his own head, the dispatches said.

The first Princeton dispatch reported that Downey's friends and "the community generally" were "very much incensed" and that lynching was freely talked of, while the sheriff considered taking Grubb to Evansville.
The Jasper Weekly Courier later wrote that the sheriff, "fearing an attack on the jail," moved him that night.
In the following days, a crowd from Downey's neighborhood twice started into Princeton and turned back on learning that Grubb was gone, and a later account placed one gathering a mile east of town.
Downey died on Sept. 19, and that night Evansville jail officers were warned of "a movement on foot in Gibson county to lynch him if possible."
Sheriff Schaum, then in Indianapolis, was summoned home, though no attack on the Evansville jail was reported.
Grubb was afterward moved to Jeffersonville, described in one news summary as the State Prison South, which added that the Princeton mob "had arranged to hang Grubb."
When Grubb was taken to Vincennes for trial on Oct. 11, masked men expected him to pass through Francisco, Downey's home station, eight miles east of Princeton.
Two scouts rode an Air-Line train from Oakland City, and when it stopped at Francisco eight men entered each coach, "inspected every face," and left without a word.
The Journal counted sixty men, and the wire reports said Sheriff McGary had taken another train.
Grubb's trial began in the Knox Circuit Court on Oct. 12, with a plea of insanity, before crowded courtrooms.
The jury found him guilty of first-degree murder and, after eight hours, fixed the death penalty, which was read to him on Oct. 19.
No arrests of the men in the mobs appear in the coverage, and as of Oct. 26 no execution date had been set.
Coverage came entirely from white papers, led by the Indianapolis Journal's special correspondents at Princeton, Evansville and Vincennes.
The Journal called Grubb "the fiend" and "the murderer" before his trial and headed the train story "A Mob of Would-Be Lynchers Boards the Wrong Train."
Its trial report noted praise for the jury's "moral courage" and treated the mob's attempt as an expression of the "indignation of Miss Downey's friends," without criticism.
In September, wire versions of the shooting and of Downey's death ran in St. Paul, Waterbury and Yankton.
The train search reached Rock Island, Wilmington and Fort Worth papers on Oct. 13.
Their headlines stressed the mob's failure, as in the Rock Island Argus's "The Lynchers Got Left" and the Fort Worth Gazette's report that "the mob was cheated of its victim."
Reports disagreed on Downey's wounds and on when she died: the Princeton special and the trial report give Sept. 19, while the Jasper Weekly Courier says the following Sunday.
Grubb was described as living at Oakland in one dispatch and at Francisco in another.

accounts.label: Princeton and Evansville specials (September)
accounts.gist: Lynching was talked of from the day of the shooting; crowds from Downey's neighborhood twice started into Princeton and turned back on learning Grubb was gone, and Evansville jail officers were warned of a plan to lynch him there.

accounts.label: Vincennes and Princeton wire (train search)
accounts.gist: Sixty masked, armed men stopped and searched a train at Francisco expecting Grubb on his way to trial at Vincennes; he had been sent by another road.

accounts.label: Indiana news summary
accounts.gist: The Princeton mob had arranged to hang Grubb and would probably have done so had he not been removed to the State Prison South.

accounts.label: Trial report and county weekly
accounts.gist: Downey's friends' indignation led to an attempt to lynch Grubb, whose neck was saved by spiriting him to Evansville; the sheriff moved him from the Princeton jail the night of the shooting, fearing an attack.

framing.detail: Indiana papers reported the mob threat as a consequence of the crime, calling Grubb 'the fiend' and 'the murderer', and the mob 'would-be lynchers' without condemning them.
Out-of-state papers ran the shooting under 'Shot His Sweetheart' and the train search under 'The Lynchers Got Left' and 'A Disappointed Mob'.

conflicts.note: The Princeton special written the day of death and the trial report agree on Sept. 19; the later county weekly's 'Sunday' is likely an error.

info: Downey shot at the Princeton fair grounds on Thursday, Sept. 13, 1888; lynching talk that day.

Princeton (fair grounds, jail; a mob gathered a mile east of town); Francisco, eight miles east of Princeton (train search); Grubb held at Evansville, then Jeffersonville (State Prison South), tried at Vincennes.
Sylvester (Syl) Grubb, 24, of Oakland, Ind., the target of the mobs; not harmed by them. Race not stated in any report.
Accused of shooting Gertrude Downey, who had refused his company and suit, at the Princeton fair grounds; she died of the wounds.
Friends of Downey and men from the neighborhood where she lived; a 'Princeton band' with a leader at Francisco; masked men.
Jury found Grubb guilty of first-degree murder and fixed the death penalty after eight hours; sentence read Oct. 19; execution date not yet fixed as of Oct. 26.
